# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical read: Two-year follow-up of the Varden trial and the Halden subset

This is a strong follow-up. It answers most of the open questions from the earlier documents: it adds an hours measure that captures unclaimed work, registers a confirmatory test of the meetings idea, runs to 24 months, and reports the Halden subset as an upper bound rather than a general estimate. Its rebuttals of Varga and Holm and of the meta-analysis are largely fair. The main weaknesses are a summary that overstates the decline, a mediation analysis presented with more certainty than it can support, and a contaminated control group that the authors describe but do not connect to their decay estimate.

## The numbers are consistent

- **24-month per-hour gains:** 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so +9.8% on timesheets. 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so +8.5% on logs.
- **Per-hour intervals:** symmetric on the log scale. The per-FTE intervals are symmetric on a linear scale (±4.6 to 4.7 points), as at nine months.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%), and 96.8 / 0.866 = 1.118, so +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Meetings change:** treated −3.5 hours, control −0.2, giving a −3.3 difference-in-differences. This matches the nine-month figure.
- **Counter staffing:** restoring per-FTE output after a fall of 11.4% needs 1/0.886 ≈ 13% more staff, close to the county's 12%. The 9% rise in cost per contact is plausible if staff costs are about three-quarters of total cost, but the paper does not explain the gap.

## What the follow-up gets right

- **Log-in data address unrecorded work.** The 24-month result uses an hours measure that catches unclaimed time. It moves the estimate only slightly (9.8% → 8.5%), so timesheets were not hiding much.
- **The meetings hypothesis is tested properly.** It was registered in advance with two named mediators and a single outcome, which is what both the nine-month report and the critics asked for.
- **The counter-arm results are now compared with control.** Waiting times are 7.3 minutes in treated offices against 4.0 in control. The arm was ended, with an estimate of what restoring service would cost. This fixes the treated-only wait comparison I flagged at nine months, and the decision to end the arm is itself strong evidence on coverage-bound work.
- **The Halden subset is described honestly.** "Survivors twice over" and "an upper bound for organisations that self-select" is the right way to describe it.
- **The meta-analysis's duration claim is checked.** The four long studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the problem I suspected: the "no decay" result came from the design features that inflate effects.
- **The paper is candid about the limits of its design.** The authors say plainly that no arm reorganised without also cutting hours.

## Problems

**1. The summary overstates the decline.**
The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". That compares a timesheet figure with a log figure. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8%, as the body says. The summary makes the decline look about 45% larger than the comparable measure shows. Nor has the decline been shown to be real. The intervals overlap heavily (6.9 to 18.4 against 4.6 to 15.2), and no test of the change between time points is reported. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. "Declined by about a quarter" is a point estimate with wide uncertainty.

**2. Contamination of the control group probably accounts for part of the decline.**
Two of the seven control offices ran their own meeting audits in month 15 and gained about 4.1% per hour. On its own, that would raise the control average by roughly 1.2%, and so shrink the treated-versus-control gap by about a point. That could explain a large share of the 2.7-point fall from 12.5% to 9.8%. The paper presents the audit as a separate observation and attributes the decline to "fading of an initial effect", without considering that the control group improved. The decay estimate should be reported with and without these two offices.

There is also a related oddity. If the two audit offices fell to 5.0 hours of meetings, the 24-month control mean of 7.0 implies the other five rose from about 7.2 to about 7.8 hours. Either that is a real rise, or the audit offices drifted back towards their old level by month 24. Either way it is worth reporting.

**3. The mediation analysis is presented with more certainty than it can bear.**
- **"Confirms" is too strong.** Mediation shares depend on the assumption that nothing unmeasured drives both meeting cuts and productivity, such as how good the office's management is. The limitations section admits this cannot be guaranteed, but the summary says the test "confirms" the shares.
- **The sample size is overstated.** The paper credits "a larger sample of office-months". Repeated months within the same 14 offices do not add independent units. If office-months were treated as independent, the intervals (28 to 66%; 2 to 34%) are too narrow. The paper needs to say how the analysis handled clustering by office.
- **The test may not be independent of the original finding.** It was registered at month 11, after the exploratory result from the same offices was known. If the outcome window includes months 1 to 9, it partly reuses the data that generated the hypothesis. A clean test would use months 12 to 24 only. The paper should state which window was used.
- **Calendar data may not capture all meeting time.** Calendars record scheduled meetings. Standing meetings that are cancelled may be replaced by ad hoc calls or messages, so the size of the meetings pathway could be overstated.
- **The audit evidence is broadly consistent.** The meetings pathway explains about 4 points (47% of 8.5%) from a cut of about 3.3 hours. The control audit gave about 4.1% from a 2.1-hour cut. Both are uncontrolled or model-based, so this is suggestive only.

**4. It is unclear what log-in time measures.**
"Active log-in time on the case-management system" may exclude meetings, phone calls and other work done off the system. If it does, it measures casework time, not total working time, and a per-hour figure based on it is not directly comparable with the timesheet figure. The baseline numbers suggest it is not purely casework: a fall of 11% is far larger than the roughly 3% fall in non-meeting time implied by the timesheets. The definition should be stated, along with whether meeting time is included, because it also affects how the meetings pathway should be read.

**5. The Halden follow-up has its own selection problem.**
- **Who responded:** only 14 of the 23 organisations contacted replied, about 61%. Organisations that struggled or reverted may have been less likely to respond, so the three reversions are probably a minimum.
- **How the reversions are labelled:** the summary says the reverters were "all with client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency cited client deadlines, which is a different problem from staffing opening hours. Grouping it as "coverage" is a label applied after the fact. It is more informative to say directly that one discretionary-sector organisation reverted, since that tempers the clean split between discretionary and coverage-bound work.
- **Who wrote it:** Okafor, an original Halden author, co-authors this section. The section is candid, but the overlap is worth noting.

**6. Some earlier gaps remain.**
- **Uncertainty:** sick days and resignations are still reported without confidence intervals.
- **Cost:** cost per case in case-processing is still not discussed. With full pay and output per FTE at −3.4%, unit labour cost in treated offices rose by roughly 3 to 4%.
- **Backlog:** the size and age of backlogs and compliance with statutory deadlines, which I flagged at nine months, are still not reported.

**7. The rebuttal of Varga and Holm is mostly fair, with one small misreading.**
Varga and Holm extrapolated self-reported energy to baseline at month ten, which on their own figures is closer to month nine. They implied, rather than calculated, that the productivity gain would vanish with it. Saying the data are "not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten" is reasonable. It reads slightly more precision into their argument than was there.

## Bottom line

This follow-up settles several questions from the earlier documents.

**Settled:**
- In discretionary public-sector casework, a gain of roughly 8 to 10% in output per hour persists at 24 months. It holds up against randomisation, record-based output and an hours measure that catches unclaimed work. "Entirely an artifact" is no longer tenable for this setting.
- Coverage-bound work loses output and service unless staffing rises. The county ended that arm, and estimated the extra cost of restoring service at about 9%.
- Cutting meetings is a plausible and probably substantial part of the gain. Fatigue appears to contribute less.

**Still open:**
- **Size of the decline:** it is probably smaller than the summary implies, given that the like-for-like measure falls only from 12.5% to 9.8% and the control group improved.
- **Mechanism shares:** the 47% and 18% depend on untestable assumptions and on clustering being handled properly.
- **Reorganisation without shorter hours:** whether the same gains are available from reorganisation alone. This is the most decision-relevant question. The two audit offices hint at a yes, but only a trial with a "reorganise without cutting hours" arm can answer it.
- **Other settings:** generalisation to private-sector, manufacturing and shift-based work remains unknown.

Across all five documents, the evidence has settled on a fairly stable picture: about a 10% gain per actual hour in discretionary work, output per worker slightly below baseline, unit labour costs modestly higher, clear losses in coverage-bound work, and the gain shrinking only modestly over two years.
